description: We’re curious problem-solvers tackling Be An Earth System Trend Detective! We’ll dig into NASA Earth data (temperature, vegetation, sea ice, air quality), find trends that matter, and turn them into clear interactive visuals. We’re friendly, organised and here to build something real. Looking for: Python/data analysis, data visualisation, front-end dev, Earth/climate science knowledge, and pitch/storytelling skills. Beginners welcome!
summary: Earth Detective is a web app that turns NASA data into clear evidence of how our planet is changing. Users pick a place and a climate variable, such as temperature, rainfall, soil moisture or snow, from NASA POWER, and the app charts it from 2000 to today. It then runs a Mann-Kendall test with Sen’s slope to say whether the trend is statistically significant, and by how much it changes each year. Satellite images from NASA Worldview show the change visually, as with the Aral Sea, which has lost 82% of its water area in a significant downward trend. A Time Machine slider, a live NASA EONET events feed and a Solutions panel link the data to real-world action. It matters because people see headlines about climate change but rarely the evidence behind them. Earth Detective lets anyone, from students to local planners, test a trend for themselves.
details:
What it does: picks a location and variable, fetches the time series from NASA POWER, plots it, and reports % change, Sen’s slope and Mann-Kendall significance (p-value). It compares Worldview MODIS imagery over time for the Aral Sea, Lake Urmia and Lake Mead, and shows current natural events from EONET.
Benefits and impact: makes Earth-system trends easy to test and understand, separating real change from noise, for education and local decision-making.
Tools: Python with FastAPI for the backend and statistics; HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the frontend; Chart.js for charts; Git and GitHub.
Creativity: it pairs a statistical significance test with satellite “before and after” images, so users see the change and the proof together.
Factors we considered: free open data with no API keys, simple design for non-experts, caching so it stays fast, and honest statistics instead of eyeballing a chart.
